items.title: 71542_Bill Coleman autobiographical manuscript
items.q: Barney Josephson did not want Al and I in his club anymore.

ctx.x: We never played behind Hazel when she did her act, but one time I suppose she wanted to see what quality the band really had because she made an arrangement on a song that she wanted us to accompany her [on] and she had it in the key of A, which put me in the key of B, which is five sharps and which is a key that is not often used in jazz. We rehearsed the number one afternoon and she put it in her programme that night. We played it down perfectly, but Hazel never called the number again. What a funny bird!

I said I would explain why I thought Lew the barman was a great person. Barney was a real liberal boss and a communist. He gave us a special price for drinks and it was Lew who served us. Al Hall and myself were the heaviest drinkers in the band. In fact we were the only two in the group that drank. Other than Yank, who smoked cigars, we were the only two in the group who smoked cigarettes. The popular drink at the moment was rum and coca cola and Lew was very heavy-handed with us when we went into the bar for a…

The 4th of October, I recorded for a singer named Eddy Howard and the group included Benny Morton on trombone, Edmond Hall clarinet, Bud Freeman, a popular white tenor man, the famous Charlie Christian on guitar, Billy Taylor, Sr., Yank Porter, and Eddie Gibbs on guitar. The 9th of December was a date with Teddy Wilson's orchestra for an ex-Benny Goodman singer named Helen Ward with George James, a baritone sax player, and Eddie Gibbs added to Teddy's group.
